around.headline: 566 motorists booked for drunk driving in a single day's crackdown
around.summary: Bengaluru traffic police booked 566 motorists for drunk driving in checks held today, per The Hindu. Enforcement is active through the evening and night, so skip driving after any drinks and book a cab instead.

around.headline: Namma Metro Pink Line's elevated stretch likely to open in September
around.summary: The elevated section of Bengaluru's Pink Line metro corridor is expected to open to the public next month, per Construction World. Worth tracking if your commute could shift to this new stretch once it's live.

around.headline: Karnataka tells Supreme Court it 'released excess water' as Cauvery dispute with Tamil Nadu resurfaces
around.summary: Karnataka told the Supreme Court it had released excess water amid Tamil Nadu's fresh Cauvery plea, even as the Kabini reservoir's level dropped 10 feet and farmers prepared to protest today, per The Times of India. A reminder that Bengaluru's water supply is tied to a river-sharing dispute that resurfaces every dry patch.

around.headline: The 'paid girl scam' is targeting lonely hearts on dating apps
around.summary: A scam where fraudsters pose as companions on dating apps and extract advance payments for meetups that never happen is gaining momentum, per The Times of India. Never wire money to someone you haven't met in person, however convincing the chat.

around.headline: India's economy posts robust growth despite Mideast energy shock
around.summary: India's economy is showing resilient growth even as Middle East tensions push up energy costs, per The Wall Street Journal. For now that's easing fears of a sharp fuel-price or job-market shock at home, though it's worth watching if the energy situation escalates.

street_smart.title: You're waiting at a Bengaluru bus stop when someone nearby suddenly collapses or clutches their chest — like today's report that BMTC bus stops have no medical aid on hand for exactly this kind of emergency. What's the single best thing to do in the first minute?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real report: BMTC bus stops across Bengaluru have no medical-aid arrangements for passengers facing an emergency (Bangalore Mirror). Medical-emergency response hasn't been used as a street-smart topic in the last three weeks of briefs, which instead covered fake job deposit fraud (08-31 morning), a dating-app meetup robbery (08-30 morning), unregulated wellness injectables (08-30 evening), BESCOM doorstep impersonation (08-29 evening), bank-OTP calls (08-29 morning), and phone snatching (08-28 evening) — none about a public medical emergency.
street_smart.situation: It's evening rush hour, the stop is crowded, and there's no BMTC staff or first-aid kit in sight — just other commuters standing around unsure what to do.

choices.text: Call 108 (Karnataka's free ambulance service) yourself right away and give the exact bus stop name or nearest landmark; start CPR or basic first aid while you wait if you're trained to.
choices.feedback: Correct. Per today's report, BMTC stops simply don't have medical aid stationed there, so waiting for transit staff to produce equipment or expertise that doesn't exist wastes the minutes that matter most. Calling 108 yourself with a precise location gets a trained team moving fastest.

choices.text: Assume the bus conductor or BMTC staff nearby will have a first-aid kit or know what to do, so wait for them to take charge.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Today's report specifically flags the absence of medical aid at BMTC stops — there is no kit or trained staff to hand this off to. Assuming otherwise means precious first minutes pass with nobody actually calling for help.

choices.text: Film the scene or post on social media appealing for an ambulance instead of calling 108 yourself.
choices.feedback: A social post might eventually reach someone who can help, but there's no guarantee of speed, and it delays the one action that reliably works: a direct call to 108 with your exact location.

choices.text: Try to move the person yourself to a nearby pharmacy or clinic instead of calling an ambulance.
choices.feedback: Moving someone with a suspected cardiac event, fracture, or head/spine injury can make things worse. Call 108 first — only move the person if there's immediate danger where they are, or if the responders on the call tell you to.

takeaways: Save 108 (Karnataka's ambulance service) in your phone now; giving a precise landmark or bus stop name when you call saves crucial minutes.
Don't assume public transit stops have first aid on hand — BMTC stops currently don't, per today's report — so you may be the only responder for those first critical minutes.
A basic CPR/first-aid course (free ones run through Red Cross and St John Ambulance chapters in Bengaluru) turns you from a bystander into someone who can actually help before the ambulance arrives.

quiz.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution lets citizens directly approach courts to enforce their Fundamental Rights?
quiz.why: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it makes Fundamental Rights directly enforceable.

quiz.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?
quiz.why: The ampere is named after André-Marie Ampère, a 19th-century French physicist who helped found the study of electromagnetism.
